config.title: How to Get Into Berghain - FAQ
config.subtitle: How the door really works, when to arrive, the rules inside, and the clubs to try instead.

items.q: How do you get into Berghain?
items.a: There is no guaranteed method, but you can load the odds. Come solo or in a small group rather than a big loud pack, stay calm and quiet in the queue, dress dark and understated, know who is playing, and bring ID. Do not film, do not turn up visibly drunk, and if you are turned away do not argue. The door is subjective and unpredictable, so treat entry as a possibility you have improved, not a prize you have earned.

items.q: What time should I arrive at Berghain?
items.a: Later than you think. Berlin has no legal closing time, so there is nothing to rush for. Arriving at 22:00 or 23:00 means standing in a queue for a near-empty room. The floors fill after 01:00 to 02:00, the peak runs from roughly 03:00 to well past 08:00, and the Klubnacht keeps going through Sunday into Monday morning. For a first night, aim to arrive in the small hours, not the evening.

items.q: What is the Berghain dress code, and how much does it cost?
items.a: There is no published dress code and no checklist that guarantees entry, but the safe register is dark, plain and practical: think black and understated rather than a going-out outfit or a slogan T-shirt. Entry to a Klubnacht is usually around 25 to 30 euros. Since late 2025 you can pay by card at the door and the bars, though the cloakroom is still cash, so carry some.

items.q: Why are photos banned inside Berghain?
items.a: Cameras are covered with a sticker at the door and phones stay away inside. The no-photo rule is not there to be mysterious; it lets people be themselves on the dancefloor without ending up in a stranger's video. It is a scene with deep queer roots, built around the music rather than spectating, and respecting the rule is part of being a guest of the space rather than a tourist.

items.q: What are good alternatives to Berghain in Berlin?
items.a: Plenty, often with friendlier doors. Sisyphos in Rummelsburg feels like a small festival with a big open-air area. Kater Blau on the Spree at Holzmarkt is relaxed and riverside. ://about blank in Friedrichshain runs strong queer-friendly nights with a garden. Tresor, in the former Kraftwerk power station, is historic Berlin techno. RSO in Schöneweide is a large warehouse. Note that Watergate closed at the end of 2024, so skip older guides that still list it.
